utterances.text: The specific objection I made was after the question relating to the publication and I understand that in the witness's statement there is a reference to the word "massacre." So although the word did jump out at me, my objection is not specifically related to that word, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So now we are -- yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's not just in the witness's statement, it's at line 7 of page 50 which is exactly why I used that word in the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Line 7, page 50, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Line 7, page 50, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But did you -- you used it in a question before that. That was the first time that the word was used, unless I'm wrong, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise. That's correct. It is after the potentially leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. This being clarified and Mr. Gosnell having understood that he has to be a little bit more cautious about the qualification of incidents, Mr. Gosnell, we are now at the stage of admitting this document. Do you have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The Prosecution indeed does object to the admission of this document on the basis that it is simply tu quoque evidence that, as Your Honours are well aware, cannot constitute an excuse for crimes within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The document discusses events at Miljevac Plateau, crimes that ostensibly appear to have been committed according to this documentation against Serbs, and the Defence simply hasn't explained the relevance and has not provided a sufficient basis for this to be admitted onto the record in these proceedings. And I note, Your Honour, this affects a large number of documents related -- in fact, a considerable proportion of this witness's evidence is pure and simple tu quoque evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Two points. One, is the word "massacre" is actually used at paragraph 25 and 26 of the witness's statement. I just wanted to put that on the record. Second point is this is not tu quoque. The purpose of adducing this evidence is understand the nature of the fears of people, in particular, at the time of the 1993 Maslenica attack which occurred six months after the Miljevacki Plateau attack. There were consequences of the Miljevacki -- of the Maslenica attack that are directly relevant to charges in the indictment and getting to the bottom of why that happened is important. At the very least, it's important context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, if I could just add one word. Your Honours, the witness's statement discusses these fears in detail of the Serb population in the RSK. This document adds nothing to that except for images and additional detail that is purely tu quoque evidence. And, Your Honours, in relation to my learned friend's submission, a lot of water passed under the bridge in between Miljevac and then Maslenica in 1993 at least six months later. Many events occurred and so it is a somewhat tenuous connection to draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked; Judge Hall dissenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the document admitted and marked, and a number will be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, at paragraphs 29 and 30, you describe the attack on Maslenica bridge and its environs, and you describe 10.000 Serb refugees having fled those areas that were targeted or taken over by Croatian forces and that 348 soldiers and civilians were killed on the Serb side during this attack. And we don't need further details on that. It's in your statement. But can you tell us over what period of time this attack took place? How long did the fighting continue in relation to this attack?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The attack began on 22nd January 1993, and the fighting went on for the whole year of 1993 in the area of Ravni Kotar. It was covered all by the operation called Maslenica. Croatian soldiers and members of the Croatian special police raided that territory and Serbs were being killed throughout that year, but, of course, most of them perished in the first four or five days. I, as chairman of the commission for exchanges, both of the living and the dead, later took over most of those bodies from the Croatian side and counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 03146, which I believe should now have a Defence exhibit number, if I'm not mistaken, since this is an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D240.234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. And that's Defence tab 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a document which is entitled: "Memo of the meeting held on 27 May 1993," under the letterhead "RSK government, State Committee for Relations with UNPROFOR." Were you a member of that committee?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to the fact that by that time I was already secretary of the government, I was also a member of the State Committee of the Republic of Serbian Krajina for relations with UNPROFOR. And I attended the meeting that produced this record, as can you see from the content of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We see what appears to be the attachment to the cover letter, which is the memo itself, memorialising the meeting that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I'd like, please, to go to page 10 in the English and page 5 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says at the second-last paragraph in the English: "To us, these are imperative issues that we cannot repudiate. The ?prospect of living together in the RH after this bloody war is over, which resulted in the third genocide in the last 75 years, gives us the right to present these facts in the way we did." Now can you explain, Mr. Strbac, what is meant here by this reference to "living together in the RH"?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, all these representatives of different international organisations who were in the Republic of Serb Krajina, and most of them were in Knin as it was the capital of the Republic of Serb Krajina were telling us, Serbs, that we had to live in the Croat state with Croats and our answer to them was that two are required for co-existence. The other side has to be willing and ready as well. Since they had killed us, over here, it says three genocides, the First World War, the Second World War, and also what preceded this meeting, that was the Miljevacki Plateau and Maslenica and Nos Kalik, and many other things that happened in 1991 and that are not referred to in my statement. We were assuring them and this document also says that this kind of co-existence is impossible in this situation because the Croats basically did not want us. If they had wanted us, they wouldn't have been persecuting us and killing us as they did. So just like for marriage, it takes two for co-existence to work as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just now in your answer you've twice used the expression "co-existence." What do you mean by co-existence?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I have been using the word "suzivot," and I don't know how they've been interpreting that. Now I heard the word "koegzistencija." Now I don't know whether that's a mistake in the interpretation. I did not mention the word "koegzistencija," I just used "suzivot."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Co-existence, living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, leaving aside the exact word used, can you help us understand what these words mean and, more importantly, how you meant them as they're set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has insisted that he used the word "suzivot," and so I think he should be asked about what he meant by that word, "suzivot," not two different words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Witness -- perhaps I could move to a different question. What is the difference in meaning between these two words, if you had to explain it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any substantive difference. I just wanted us to stick to the term that we had used. I don't see any substantive difference. Probably the content should be the same within these two concepts the way I understand them. I tried to explain what "suzivot" means. Before the war, in Tito's Yugoslavia we did have this "suzivot" where we all lived together, all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia in some brotherhood and unity, if I can put it that way. At least that's how I felt. I don't know about others but that's how I felt. I worked and lived among Croats, I worked as a judge, and I tried all irrespective of ethnicity, and now all of a sudden, we were in a position to be expelled from work. They asked me to sign some kind of statements of loyalty to the new state. Many others were asked to do even worse things. Yet others were not asked for anything. They were simply kicked out of the police or other authorities or different companies. I know that because I defended quite few of people as a lawyer. There were different proceedings involved, disciplinary, et cetera, so this is no longer any kind of life together or co-existence. As I've said, both sides have to be willing and ready to live together. The Croat people obviously as the majority people did not feel that way because had they felt that way, they wouldn't have done what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But in this document that's in front of us, are you using the terms -- I should first ask you is the word "suzivot" or "koegzistencija" used in the original?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: We used precisely that word "sazivot." That is the Serbian version of "suzivot." So that would be the that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were you expressing, by using this word, any view about where people of a particular ethnicity could live?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, no. When I accepted to be secretary of the government in the Bjegovic government, that was towards end of April 1993, that is to say, after the Maslenica operation, of course, we did talk and we tried to reach agreement. I did know about Bjegovic's programme and the government programme. We had had enough of a war. We needed a life in peace, to develop the economy. We did not want to expel anyone from the Republic of the Serb Krajina; that is to say, that we wanted to create a state of our own where, I mean, people could live, irrespective of religious or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this word "suzivot" and the agenda that you've just described as being reflected in that word, did you express that and did your colleagues on the state committee express that on other occasions to UNPROFOR officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the question contains the suggested and hoped for answer. So it's, by definition, leading, and there isn't a foundation in the lead-up of questions to put it in such a narrowly leading way. It could have been asked in a broader way as to whether it had been used on other occasions and then asked, with whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll allow the question. Please continue, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were talking about everyone and these were meetings that were held every day at all levels. When I was present at some joint meetings with the prime minister, I listened to how this was discussed. When we attended meetings of this committee for relations with UNPROFOR, when I chaired meetings or when I led delegations of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, I talked about that. So once again "suzivot," it pertained to two already separated states: The Republic of the Serb Krajina that hadn't been internationally recognised but obviously it was recognised as an entity because resolutions were passed concerning it in the United Nations; on the other hand, there was the Republic of Croatia that was a recognised state. We were at war and we said that it was impossible for the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Croatia to become one again. As for "suzivot" with Croats and everybody else in the Republic of Serbian Krajina that was never brought into question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slow down for the record and for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, could you please just slow down a little bit so that the interpreters and transcribers can get your words down accurately please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we move now, please, to page 17 of the English of this document. Page 8 of the B/C/S. And can I go back and ask you now, Mr. Strbac, do you remember that you did participate in formulating or writing this memo?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I believe that I did participate. It's hard to remember given the time distance. But I am fully familiar with the content which means that I took part in the preparations as well. Well, this happened every day, these meetings. It was war time. This state committee, the government, we were in permanent session, as we say, and it's not that just two or three people got together and compiled a document and handed it over to these officials from UNPROFOR. Rather, quite simply this was discussed every day, day in, day out, for months, and this is the result of all of these discussions and debates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you say that "this was discussed every day, day in, day out, for months." Were you referring to the state committee's contacts with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I'm also referring to the state organs of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, the government, this committee, and all these other organs, because there had to be frequent communication. Also there was daily communication with different representatives. Knin and Krajina were full of these international representatives. You could not walk down the street without bumping into one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says here at point 6 that: "The RSK requests a definitive answer to the question whether the Vance Plan is still in existence. As far as we are concerned, it is still a legally valid document, regardless of the resolutions adopted subsequently." Do you remember what lay behind this question? Why was this question posed, whether the Vance Plan is still in existence?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The Serbs from the Republic of Serb Krajina had difficulty in accepting the Vance Plan. There were divided views on this. Finally the Vance Plan was signed because it did not prejudge a political solution of the conflict. However, when the Vance Plan was accepted, when UNPROFOR arrived, things became troublesome for the Serbs. Aggressions of the Croat army started. We mentioned some of them today: Nos Kalik in March when UNPROFOR was being deployed, and then we also mentioned the Miljevac Plateau in June, and then Maslenica in 1993, in January. It seems to me that the Security Council would pass a resolution for each and every one of these occurrences, and these resolutions somewhat deviated from the Vance Plan. It became obvious that this political solution was being prejudged in a way and that they were returning us to the Croatian state. And that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Witness, I am convinced and very sure that the interpreters can't follow you properly. You are speaking way too fast. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they're not complaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Might be time for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I've lost my train of thought, it seems ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think that last intervention of you, Mr. Strbac, is totally inappropriate. I asked you to slow down. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I indeed see the time. We'll take our first break, 30 minutes -- or the second break, sorry, 30 minutes, Mr. Witness, and we'll be back at 12.45. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, just before the break, you were referring to "Security Council resolutions that deviated from the Vance Plan in a way that they were returning us to the Croatian state." Now just very specifically, can you recall what measures being adopted by the Security Council were raising doubts as to whether the Vance Plan was still applicable?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, for example, as far as I can remember, after the Maslenica operation, a resolution was passed according to which the Croats were supposed to withdraw, the Croatian forces were supposed to withdraw from the area that had been taken. The Serbs were supposed to return weapons into the arms depots under this double lock, double key. The Serbs did not return their weapons as the Croats did not withdraw. It seems to me that some other resolutions were also passed which refer to some customs law or something like that, namely, that all exports and imports should go through Croatia for the Republic of the Serb Krajina, which was mind-boggling, especially at a time of war and when hostilities had peaked. So people came from these international organisations, they talked to us about how within Croatia we would have autonomy like, I don't know, southern Tyrol in Italy and then the Aland Islands in Finland. They took our people to seminars in different places in the world. So all this implied we should go back to Croatia, whereas we were staying that political issues had to be resolved, that the Vance Plan did not prejudge any political solution, and the Croats were not exactly in favour of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 01594, Defence tab 77, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we only have this document, Mr. Strbac, in English uploaded, but it is an outgoing cable from Wahlgren to Annan dated the 19th of April, 1993. So approximately a month before the memorandum of your meeting with Mr. Stoltenberg. And the subject line reads: "Consequences for our mandate in Croatia of recent Security Council resolution on sanctions meeting with prime minister designate Bjegovic of the RSK." Can I first ask you, do you recall hearing about any meetings from Mr. Bjegovic that he may have had with Mr. Wahlgren around this time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I heard that he held meetings with UNPROFOR and all other representatives of international organisations as prime minister designate, and he talked to them as he talked to me when he was trying to talk me into joining his government as secretary or some minister. I did not want to be a minister. I heard about this type of discussion, namely, that we would join this government, take over this government, and create a normal state, but that that is impossible if the representatives of international organisations are not on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this document says at point 1: "We are increasingly concerned over the disparity between actions being taken in New York and realities on the ground. We find -- we had already expressed our grave concern with regard to paragraph 12 of the new Sanctions resolution ... in the hope of averting a major setback to our mandate in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then, please, if we could turn over to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At the bottom of paragraph 6, after referring to some resolutions, it says: "The new resolution made it clear that the basic tenets of the Vance Plan were being brushed aside. This was a further step to impose Croatian authority on them." And at the bottom the very last sentence on this page: "Does the Vance Plan still exist? We do not know, nor do we know by what it has been replaced, except a lot of anti-Serb huffing and puffing which damages us much more than them." Did you hear from Mr. Bjegovic whether he heard from any UNPROFOR officials whether they were in doubt as to whether the Vance Plan was still in effect?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now. I cannot give just a yes or no answer to this. But I think that I have responded earlier on when I said that Bjegovic was saying that he had meetings as prime minister designate with all the representatives, all representatives of all international organisations, and that the basic topic of discussion with all of them was precisely the Vance Plan. You must understand that throughout Krajina there was an UNPROFOR presence, inkblots, and I already said that we Serbs found it hard to accept but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry for cutting you off, Mr. Strbac, but I just want to try to refocus you back on my question, if I may, and proceed in this way. How did Mr. Stoltenberg respond when the -- when the issue was raised of whether the Vance Plan was still in effect during your meeting in May with him?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they didn't know either, whether this plan was in existence or not. And I assumed that that is why they wrote such letters, that they were not sending to us. They were sending these letters to their superiors in New York and wherever because they themselves were perplexed over the situation on the ground. We have the Vance Plan that we accepted. We have peacekeeping forces on the ground and something else is being decided in New York. We can all see, they can see, we can see, under our pressure, that they are asking their superiors, they're asking the Security Council to respond and say what's going on. Does the Vance Plan still exist? How should they behave on the ground? They don't know, and how could we know then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D245, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 63 of your statement, you described meeting with Mr. Bjegovic and being offered and taking the position of secretary of the RSK government. Can you ask you, first of all, to describe briefly, if you can, your duties as secretary of the government?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: First of all, the secretary of the government is not a member of the government. It is ministers who are members of the government, as well as the prime minister. So I was there in a technical capacity. That meant that I had a few people there in the secretariat, I also had a deputy, I also had various clerks. And we were supposed to prepare government meetings and we were supposed to record government meetings, write up all the decisions that were reached at meetings of the government. We did not transcribe meetings at the time. We just wrote up brief conclusions from the taped material and that would become part of the record that would be approved at the following session if there were no objections. So all of this material, all these decisions, would be submitted to the Official Gazette as well because, for the most part, they were published in the Official Gazette. All the ministries provided us with material for government sessions and we would then include in the agenda things that were submitted to us by the ministries. That would be it in the briefest possible terms. I was secretary of the government and also the president of the government commission for the exchange of prisoners and mortal remains. I did that before I became secretary of the government. Once I became secretary of the government, I established a commission for the entire Republic of the Serb Krajina. Before that there were different commissions at municipal, local levels, regional and so on, military, civilian, et cetera. Once I became secretary of the government, I managed to establish a single commission for the entire Republic of the Serb Krajina. Soon I also founded an NGO, Veritas, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, and that's -- and those subjects are covered in your statement, Mr. Strbac, so I won't go into all of those. But I would like to ask you how frequent were your contacts as the secretary of the government with Prime Minister Bjegovic and the other ministers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The prime minister mostly because our offices were right next door to each other. So my people did all the work that was required by the prime minister, my people from the secretariat. He just had one lady who was his secretary and I wasn't her boss. All the rest was done by my people. We worked for the prime minister. I've already said that these were contacts or, rather, preparations. And after all, there was a state of war there, and we were constantly in session so there were no special working hours. We worked day and night. Our people went out into the field, but we communicated, we talked a great deal. We were close, he and I, because I had other prime ministers that I was not that close to, but I was close to him and we shared a lot. Perhaps some things that one would not exactly expect between a prime minister and the secretary of the government, who was, after all, not an elected official.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And after you assumed the position of secretary of the government, what percentage of government sessions did you attend, would you say?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, it was a rare session that I did not attend. I remember several times it was more important for me to go to exchanges of prisoners. That could be the only reason why I didn't go to a meeting, to a government session. When exchanges had already been agreed with the Croatian side, not only with Bjegovic but others too, because I remained, until the very fall of Krajina, that would be the only times that I didn't attend the government sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how were judicial appointments made in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, we had the regular way, when there was no imminent threat of war and no state of war was declared, appointments were made by the assembly. And during the imminent threat of war and the state of war, I remember but I also refreshed my memory with some documents, the president of the republic exercising his constitutional powers, because in times of the state of war or imminent threat of war, he assumed the powers of the parliament and transferred them to the government. So while I was secretary of the government, I remember that the government appointed judges and prosecutors but that was when a state of imminent threat of war or state of war was declared. That is to say, after the Maslenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have P3093, please. Defence tab 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And before that comes up, did that method of appointment that you've just described apply to all judicial positions?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The number again is P3093.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now these appear to be the minutes from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- government session of the 16th of September, 1993, in Knin. And if we go over now to the very last page of this document, whose is the last name there on that attendance list?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It's my name. Number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could back, please, one page in both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There are a series of decisions on the appointment of judge, jurors at the Vukovar Supreme Court, on the appointment of a judge at the Knin Municipal Court, of a judge of the Knin District Court, relieving the president of the Okucani Municipal Court, and an appointment of the judge at the Slunj Municipal Court. How were the appointees decided upon, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The proposal came from the competent ministry, in this case, the Ministry of Justice, and the government decided, based on the presidential decree from sometime in January, and the president transferred his own powers and the powers of the assembly to the government. This government session took place while the Medak pocket operation was still under way. It was always the competent ministries that suggested appointments within their field of work, but the government had to formally approve it at their sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 66 of your statement, you say: "As far as I know, Goran Hadzic hardly ever came to Knin during the time that I was secretary of the government. During my tenure as secretary, he perhaps came to Knin three times, and he never attended any government session, nor was he expected to under the constitution or for any other reason." I'd like to ask you now generally what role, in practice, based on your direct observation or any conversations with the prime minister or other ministers, what role did Mr. Hadzic have in government decisions?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, none. I came in end April 1993, and in January he already left his position as president, so it was a very brief period that we coincided, but I don't remember that any materials came from the president in preparation for government sessions. It says here in this paragraph that there was a proposal to dismiss certain ministers, and perhaps that's the only time when a proposal by President Hadzic was discussed at government sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were ministers giving any reports to President Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm certain that it was not done through the secretary of the government or the secretariat. They may have had another channel along military lines or different lines, but whether they used it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've described having a close relationship with Prime Minister Bjegovic. Did he tell you that he reported to President Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Again, I have to say that he did not, through the secretariat or the secretary of the government. I don't know if he had a personal communication with him, he never told me about it. And government sessions discussed more than once, especially during the state of war and the aggression by Croatia, that the president, the head of state, should appear in Knin where all the authorities were, except for the Supreme Court. Only the president and the Supreme Court were in the eastern part, in Vukovar. All the other state bodies were in Knin, and it was logical for the president to come where all the others were. It was a time when the Medak pocket operation and Maslenica operation were still going on. But he didn't show up at government sessions, and it was never written anywhere that he had to. I believe there are even some minutes and documents where I saw that Prime Minister Bjegovic said that six different invitations had been sent to him and the president always said that he could not come because of something that was going on in Banja Luka. To be quite clear, from Vukovar to Knin, he could not travel across RSK territory because the eastern part where he worked and lived was physically cut off from the western part, from Knin, and since he didn't dare travel through Croatia, he could only travel part of the way through Serbia and part of the way through Republika Srpska. At the time of the Medak pocket operation, there was some sort of insurgency in Republika Srpska and almost as if it had been agreed with the Croats, it coincided with the Medak pocket action. It started on the same day and ended on the same day. Both of them began on the 9th of September and ended on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, since you've raised it I'll ask you about the six invitations that you just described to President Hadzic by Prime Minister Bjegovic. Were those invitations all in respect of something particular and over what time-period were those invitations made?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Since this Bjegovic government came after the Maslenica operation and the Medak pocket and that event that required the president to be with the other organs in Knin, that is the Medak pocket operation of the 9th of September, and I believe those invitations were during the state of war. From 9 to 17th September was this operation and it lasted exactly the same time as the Serbian insurgency. Several hundreds troops and officers with tanks blocked all access roads to Banja Luka, and Hadzic, as the head of state, since this insurgency was a rebellion against the corruption in the leadership of Republika Srpska, they were not able to pass too, and Hadzic was not allowed to pass because people made some connection between him and the leadership of Republika Srpska, probably because of his very office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's please turn back to page 2 of the English in this document. And in B/C/S it may be page 2. Perhaps we could just turn back to the previous page in the B/C/S. Sorry, we did need page 2, after all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now just at the top the page there in B/C/S and in English in the second paragraph, there's a -- some words attributed to Prime Minister Bjegovic, he describes what is happening around Divoselo. Is Divoselo related to the Medak pocket operation that you've been describing?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The Medak pocket operation targeted three villages, and one of them is Divoselo. Among the Serbian people, Divoselo is held as a symbol of suffering, both in the Second World War and in the last war, and many people, instead of referring to the Medak pocket, they say Divoselo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "As for the conclusions from the session held on 13 September, it is my duty to inform you that letters have been sent to the prime ministers of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro. We sent President Hadzic six invitations to appear in Knin, but he replied that could not come due to the situation in Banja Luka." Does that correspond to what you were describing earlier about Mr. Hadzic being blocked at Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely. Nobody could pass through during those days. Banja Luka was surrounded by tanks, not enemy tanks but Serb tanks. It was a rather notorious mutiny of Serb troops and officers who were angry about the corruption and the crime, from 9 to 17 September, that is to say, the same period as the Medak pocket, and there was absolutely no chance for anybody to pass through, especially not the president of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have P1914, please, which is Defence tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, these are the minutes of the 44th RSK government session dated 4th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we please turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Whose signature, if you can read it, appears at number 18?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It's my signature. You can see very well, Savo Strbac, and my signature. It's under number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could please go back to page 6 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. I apologise, we'll have to go back to page 3 of the English. And it should be page 4 or 5 of the B/C/S. Just under item 1. Yes, we'll have to go back one more page, I think, in the B/C/S. I'm afraid it must be back further. Well, to make this easy, let's go back right to the beginning page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now here we have a set of agenda items, Mr. Strbac. Can I first ask you, just reviewing this -- these agenda items, do they fall within the purview of the government's responsibility as you understood it and as you observed it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: All this falls within the agenda and the purview of the government. Not all of this is about making decisions. One part are decisions but there are briefings and all sorts of reports and information. The government can always deliberate on various issues and take up positions. It's different when decrees and decisions are made. This we see under number 3. All this fell within the purview of the government, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we just go back one page in English because it's not showing agenda item 1. Or perhaps scroll up. Yes. Agenda item 1, discussing documents relating to resolving the relations with the Presidency of the FRY, Serbia and Montenegro. And then if we turn to the page and go to the very bottom of the second page in English, we see there - very bottom - a heading saying: "Item 1." And then if we can turn the page in English one more, that's where I'd like to stay for a moment. In B/C/S, if we can go forward to the next page. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that this initial discussion which you see in front of you concerns item 1, discussing documents relating to resolving relations with the Presidency of the FRY, Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we can just go to the end of this section, which is page 6 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now this appears at the bottom of the discussion by the members of the government and there's a decision. And the decision says: "Prepare a cover letter for these topics, which would have to be signed by President Hadzic." Now, can you explain why it is that the government is asking -- on what basis is the government asking for this letter to be signed by President Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Because the letter is sent out to other states, and a state is internationally represented by the head of state, not the head of government. This is not an order to the president that he has to sign something. It's simply his constitutional responsibility to read the document and sign it. If he believes -- if he finds that he shouldn't sign it, he will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember what constitutional provision is relevant here?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: If I can think of it off the cuff, I believe it would be Article 78, para 1, item 3. I'm speaking off the top of my head, but it must be easy to check the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have L3. Defence tab 65, page 23 of the English, and page 7 of the B/C/S. Now I am afraid --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wrong. It's item 4. But it is, indeed, Article 78, paragraph 1. Item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So is it your understanding that it was on that basis that Mr. Hadzic was asked to sign the letter?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have P3803, please, which is Defence tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I wonder if my learned friend means 3083, tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That is quite right. I thank my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now this is another set of minutes of the government of the RSK, Mr. Strbac. This is the 46th Session held in Knin on the 13th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, now to page 23 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This section reads: "Before reading out the government's standpoint on an all-Serbian Assembly, Prime Minister Bjegovic stated that no one from the Republic of Serbia had issued an official order to have goods from the RSK sent back from the border." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we turn, please, to page 25 in the English and it should be the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Conclusion," and this follows the discussion by various ministers, including Martic, Kuzet, Arbutina, and so forth. The conclusion is: "The final text of the RSK government standpoint on an all-Serbian Assembly shall be drafted by the RSK Ministry of Justice and Administration." Now given Article 78, 4, which is supposed to confer authority on the president to carry out duties regarding relations with other countries, why is this being taken up by the government without any apparent reference to the authority of the president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, there can be several reasons. First of all, this is the position of the government, not a decision by the government. A position can be taken by the parliament, by the head of state. The question is now who makes the final decision, but at any rate, the government can take positions on all matters, including this all-Serbian Assembly. Secondly, the president wasn't really asked a lot about things like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'm done with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 66 of your statement, and you've already referred to this previously in your testimony, concerning the issue of the president's power to remove government ministers, and you say: "I believe that could only be done on the order of the prime minister upon a vote of the RSK Assembly." Do you remember whether there was any constitutional provision applicable to the removal of ministers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: In the article that we looked at, Article 78 of the constitution, there is some reference to the powers of the head of state when there is an imminent threat of war and when a state of war is declared. As far as I can remember, what is written there is that in that situation, the president can also change the powers and composition of all institutions in the state, including the government; therefore, ministers included. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at L3, please, again; page 27 in the English and this should be page 8 in the B/C/S. And we're looking for Article 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says that: "The president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina can propose the dismissal of some of the members of the government." Does that jog your memory as to the nature of the president's power in relation to removing ministers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness gave an answer as to which powers he thought the president could remove ministers under and the reference to this article has clearly been used in a leading way, in fact, the Defence counsel expressly said: "Does this jog your memory." So I just note for the record that this was framed in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you hear my question, Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. There are two situations. One is when it happens in peacetime and I think that this pertains to peacetime, 87; whereas Article 88, some paragraph there, speaks of the powers of the president when an imminent threat of war is declared or a state of war. That is the only way in which I can interpret that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And otherwise the removal of ministers is governed by that provision in front of you; correct? In Article 87?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we go back, please, to page 19 of this document and page 6 of the B/C/S, item 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that have any relevance to the issue?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It says here elects and -- it has to do with peacetime, yes, the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go, please, to page 27 of this document, which, again, Article 87, and it's B/C/S page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The very first line reads: "The government and every member of it are responsible for their work to the president of the republic and the assembly." Now, did this provision reflect the reality in respect of the president? Were the members of the government responsible for their work to the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: While I was in the government, I would not say -- well, we had this one situation that we discussed. There was this proposal concerning the state of war or imminent threat of war. That was in the immediate aftermath of the Medak pocket and then in 1993 when the president withdrew that proposal of his. As for these other peacetime situations, between these different actions that called for a state of war, I don't think that, in practice, he interfered with the work of the government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we turn to page 23 of the document; page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is under Article 78, under the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and item 7 reads: "Under his initiative or under the government's proposal, during the state of war or immediate threat of war, adopts acts about issues from the assembly's jurisdiction and is required to submit them before the assembly as soon as the assembly is able to meet." Do you remember that provision, Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I do. I mean, that is a provision that is studied even in law school. I'm a lawyer myself. It's nothing new. It's nothing special, just from the constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Every country has that in its constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was that provision applied in practice in 1993, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I do not recall that the president used this right, except for that one attempt that I referred to, that is part of the record of one government session, that could be considered as being under this article, when he did not agree to have two ministers replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer, Mr. Strbac, because you refer to this being as a right that appears to be conferred on the president whereas this provision is referring to a requirement, obliging him to submit acts to the assembly as soon as the assembly is able to meet; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, this sounds --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- more like cross-examination than direct examination. Quoting from the provision and attempting to force the witness to agree with that is purely leading. So, again, I'd put that on the record. The answer is now out but I would put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I recall what you said the other day, that during the Defence case, it certainly ought to be within our latitude to present matters that are at the core of the Prosecution's case to witnesses to hear their comment. I really don't know how else to present an issue for the witness's comment other than the manner in which I did it. I do regret having used that rather forceful, those forceful words at the end, but the witness's answer was ambiguous, and I think it was legitimate to seek a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now before you were cut off, you said: "Absolutely." Did you wish to say anything further, Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: This is what my answer would be: Well, what is written here is quite clear, what this provision says, that is. I said that as far as I can remember, the president, President Hadzic did not use these powers except in one particular situation. However, since these persons were not replaced, then it wasn't necessary for him to turn to the assembly and to ask for approval. That is it, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac, at paragraph 55 of your statement, you describe -- and surrounding paragraphs, you describe the process for authorising the departure of civilians from the area of the RSK, and you say there that: "The process was more or less modelled on exchange of prisoners in the sense that EUMM, UNPROFOR, UNCIVPOL, and/or the Red Cross were always involved in these movements." Now can I ask you, did they encourage contacts with the -- between the two sides on this issue?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, the answer would be yes. All these international organisations cared a lot about the protection of human rights, the protection of human lives on all sides. Since I was in charge of this commission of the Republic of Serbian Krajina for exchanges of the living and dead, sometimes we called it the commission for humanitarian issues, sometimes for the exchange of prisoners, I had daily communication with all of them. Sometimes even several times a day with the same people. I helped people get the necessary permits as I used or abused the powers that I had as secretary of the government so that I could reach all the state organs. It was easier for me that way than if I did -- had not held that position. So, you see, it wasn't that easy to -- to cross the line of separation or the front line, whatever you wish to call it. Always certain permits had to be obtained regardless of who it was that was carrying out the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now what criteria did you apply, if any, for determining whether someone should be given the necessary permits?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, the first and basic thing was that people would make these communications. My colleague, Mr. Kuzetic [phoen] and I used to have a law office before the war together, and when there was no communication between Croatia and the Krajina except through sights on weapons, as people say, we had this communication and we were helped by the international organisations, and we used their communications with the other side. And when somebody would come to us, for example, a Croat, and if he'd say that he is afraid, that he feels insecure, that he is receiving threats, that he has relatives on the other side, sons, anybody that he wished to cross over, then we would try to grants their wishes. Again, there were some objective situations like, say, Miljevac Plateau, not to mention everything that happened. There were many, many Serb refugees from Croatia. And there was this objective danger looming over Croats because people had come from the other side and then people would reach agreements amongst themselves. They would say: Well, why don't you give me the property that you left behind, and I will take over your property here. And then we tried to let this happen. And then there were people who wanted to cross to the Serb side. Just like Croats in the Krajina, Serbs in Croatia felt threatened. So that's why I'm saying that all of this happened on the basis of a system for exchange of prisoners. It's not that we ever handed over anything to the Croats without asking for something in return because objectively this happened on both sides. There wasn't any major difference. I can tell that you, in 1993, there were 130.000 refugees registered, those who had fled from Croatian-controlled territory. That perhaps doesn't sound like a lot, but if all of Krajina had a population of about 400.000, that -- then that is a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were there any -- were there any time-periods when departures were more frequent or more numerous than others?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After these operations, we were saying that in the Maslenica operation about 10.000 Serbs were expelled. They came to the municipality of Benkovac and Knin, and there were still quite a few mixed villages there, Croat/Serb. Then people went there on their own and they were trying to find places where they could stay. At that time, since this is in my area where I lived, the municipality of Benkovac, Maslenica actually included my municipality as well, so I know a lot of these people who were fleeing from their villages. And for this Crisis Staff of Benkovac where I worked, we managed to find accommodation for some people in places that were collective centres, like the elementary school and other places. There weren't very many such locations. Others were staying in the villages. They were milling about. It was hard to keep masses of people under control because 10.000 people is a lot, their families, and once they would get to a village, then -- well, the Croats would say: Well, I'm not under threat now, but I see how many of them keep coming in, and somebody is going to come tomorrow or the day after tomorrow and ask me to leave and it's better for me to leave now rather than lose my property and lose my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you try to encourage these people to stay where they resided at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: As much as possible, we were saying this will not go on for a long time, this is temporary. However, people knew best what they felt and how they felt. They would say to us that they wanted to leave until all of this blows over. We were encouraging others, saying that all of this was temporary, that it was important to save people's lives, and that property can be resolved easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D3786, please, which is Defence tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How would you characterise the nature of your relationship with your counterparts on the Croatian side in this enterprise of facilitating departures of civilians, from each side to the other?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I wrote about that and spoke about that in public over the years. We who were involved in these humanitarian affairs could just take people's word for it, and they could just take my word for it. We did not sign any documents, and, if we did, it happened very seldom. Because there was the problem of state recognition. For instance, I would like every document to say that I am a representative of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and the Croats would say: Well, we don't recognise that state, and then there would be a problem. Well, then we took everybody's word for it. Recognition is a formality but let us get the job done. Let these people get out of prison. Let us get the deceased to their families so that they can bury them properly. As for those who wished to leave, well, they were saying that they wanted to save their lives so they should leave on time. And once the war is over - we all knew that one day the war would be over - then they should return to their property alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 47, you're talking about prisoner exchanges, not civilian departures, and you describe there the difference between a one-for-one system of exchange and other grounds for exchange. And is it true that the one-for-one exchange system was applied for prisoners of war, or combatants?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: We had two rules. One was one for one; and the other one was all for all. When everybody agreed to all for all, again, it would boil down to one for one. Because the other side was always asked for more than what the other side had admitted to having. They were asking, say, for people who were no longer among the living or who went abroad and so on. So it would always be that number. We'd always have to compile lists in advance. Regardless of what we call the principle, we would have to compile a list of these persons who would be exchanged, and an exchange would hardly ever take place if everybody was not present, unless there was a very strong reason for someone not being there. If one proceeds from that principle, one for one, then what I described in my statement would happen. Namely, at first, in 1991, 1992, and even in 1993, the Serbs always had more Croat soldiers in their prisons than the Croats had Serbs, so then when you say one for one, then Croats would start arresting civilians and then they'd bring them to the exchange and they'd say: Well, there you go, one for one. That's why I was against that. Then civilians would get arrested and they would show up there as prisoners to be exchanged for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought I would have had time to complete the document, but perhaps it would be best to finish it tomorrow, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Strbac, this is -- 2.00 is the end of the -- today's hearing. We expect you to be back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. In the meantime, you remain a witness and you remain under oath. In this system, this means that you are not allowed to speak with anybody about your testimony, not even to your family back home, and also that you are not allowed to have contact with any of the parties, as long as you are under oath and on the witness stand. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of October, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
